Good morning, colleagues. Should we start, perhaps? So let me call to order this informal consultation of the Ad Hoc Working Group on Mandate Implementation Review. On behalf of my co-chair, Ambassador Wallace, and myself, I have the pleasure to welcome all of you to this session. Following our initial consultations with you on the 2nd of June on the criteria to —guide decisions on renewal, adaptation, merger, replacement, and retirement of GA mandates, and on the modalities to guide the review of existing stock of mandates, we would like to use this opportunity to discuss the next steps. You have received and reviewed our non-paper, which was circulated on the 12th of June. And we have also had the opportunity for informal and constructive exchange of views with several delegations in our hybrid workshops on 16th and 18th of June. So, colleagues, we will return to the discussion from the workshops in detail a bit later, but we thought it important to respond to one common thread from deliberations, the identified need for more information in order for member states in our decision-making on mandates, and the steps they are taking to respond to— oh, sorry, I'm on the wrong line of the manuscript. Let me start again. We need more information in order for member states to take informed decisions on mandate implementation review. We have heard this message loud and clear. Accordingly, we have asked the Secretariat to provide an update on the various things that they have been working on to support Member States in our decision-making on mandates, on the steps they are taking to respond to our requests from Resolution 18251. In addition to this update today, we— We also intend to facilitate a more in-depth technical briefing later on, specifically on the mandate registry and other elements. This would be to have a dedicated exchange with the Secretariat on what is and isn't working for delegations. But for today, I will actually hand the floor to Under-Secretary-General Guy Ryder, who is joining us on video from Turin in Italy. So, dear Guy, please take the floor.

Well, thank you very much indeed, co-chairs, and thank you for the opportunity to make this presentation remotely to the Working Group. Members of the Working Group, General Assembly Resolution 80/251 provides a practical framework for moving to better mandate creation, better implementation, and better evidence-based review. It also sets out the principle that decisions on mandates are the exclusive prerogative of member states. Uh, the resolution also addresses several requests to the Secretary-General on which I would like to take the opportunity, uh, to update you today at the request of the co-chairs, and that means that I will speak to paragraphs 3, 6, 8, 16, 18, 19, and 24 of the resolution. This said, the resolution gives us not just a set of instruction but also points the way to a new way of working. Clearer mandates, better evidence, and more disciplined follow-through. And I think that this broader perspective is important because if we treat these requests simply as a one-off exercise, we might miss the opportunity for the culture of continuous improvement that the General Assembly has aspired to create. We will therefore provide the requested information on the implementation of specific mandates at time of decision-making while respecting, of course, the diverse nature of mandates and of governance structures. Now, to turn to specific paragraphs, co-chairs. In paragraphs 8 and 16 of the resolution, the General Assembly asked the Secretary-General to improve our reporting to you, our member states. And here we are making, I think, good progress on two fronts. First, general enhancements to make our reports more focused, and more user-oriented. Over the past weeks, we have worked internally to achieve a new level of quality in reporting, and the Secretary-General will request author departments to make greater use of shorter update reports when a full report is not required in every reporting cycle, to apply more word limit and drafting discipline to reduce unnecessary repetition, and to incorporate more user-centered design approaches to make greater use of data whilst maintaining transparency and, of course, comprehensive coverage. Over time, we believe that this can make reports easier to read, easier to process, and easier to follow up. Secondly, We are looking at opportunities to optimize the portfolio of reports in accordance with paragraph 16 of the resolution. We will continue to implement all reporting mandates but remain mindful of the burden of proliferating reports. And I won't go into too much detail today because we will soon be in a position to share a note with you that sets out our approach to improved reporting overall. But let me just illustrate our approach through a couple of examples. Some reports, for example, cover major construction projects that have now largely concluded and could be brought together into a single report with a final report on completion. Others— mainly other reports— others present mainly data which is now held in continuously updated databases, and users could simply be pointed to those live sources, keeping the information current and without a separate annual compilation report. Overall, in this way, we hope that the benefits from all of these improvements will allow us to deliver better products amid severe resource constraints acting on you, our member states, and on us. Where the Secretary-General has the authority to proceed with improvements to reporting, he will do so and update the Working Group accordingly. Where a decision is to be made by an intergovernmental organ, the Secretary— the Secretariat will present suggestions at the earliest opportunity, the next opportunity, whenever and wherever discussions on draft resolutions and decisions take place so that member states have the evidence that they need for fully informed decision-making. Information on how such recommendations were, um, developed will be shared with the working group later in the year once these discussions on draft resolutions and decisions have taken place in the relevant intergovernmental organs. Let me move on to possible mechanisms for collective mandate implementation reviews. This is paragraph 18 of the resolution. The Secretariat is compiling a background note on existing mechanisms that may be relevant to collective mandate implementation reviews, and we expect that this note will be ready by the end of July. It will outline existing mechanisms including relevant practice from the Ad Hoc Working Group on the Revitalization of the Work of the General Assembly and the Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations. The purpose is not to prescribe a model, but to place existing models before you as intergovernmental organs consider how best to design review arrangements. Moving on to engagement with member states on the concept notes. This is paragraphs 3 and 6 of the resolution. Let me begin by thanking the co-chairs for circulating the templates for the concept notes. Several delegations have been in touch with us in the Secretariat asking for our input on technical Secretariat focal points, the mandate implementation landscape, and possible financial implications. We have already seen the first concept notes that have been circulated, and based on this initial experience, we are organizing the support that we can provide to you. And I'm pleased to say that we've established a new email address. It is mandates@un.org for any questions that you may have in this regard. Any delegation is welcome to reach out to our team and we will do our very best to respond. And we will soon share more information on this area in writing. We have also launched a first directory of secretariats across the UN system and will develop it in coming months, adding further contacts. Information will be provided to you through a standardized process that can help proposals be understood, signed, costed, and tracked across the mandate lifecycle. Our aim again is to make the Secretariat easier to navigate— one entry point, clear routing, and more consistent support across the entire mandate lifecycle. That brings us to the next point. This is engagement with member states. On the evidence base across the mandate lifecycle. Paragraph 24. We have heard your feedback at recent meetings of the working group as well as during the workshops. And as requested in paragraph 24, we will expand the registry as a comprehensive, regularly updated reference tool, including General Assembly, Security Council, and ECOSOC resolutions. We will also extend an invitation to publish resolutions and decisions of other organs in the same registry based on, based on interoperable standards. As is possible with the current version already of the registry, where resolutions in the registry are cited in a budget proposal, we will identify the relevant linkages. We are also exploring better digital tools to make data on activities, resources, and results available so that member states can connect each element on the chain from mandate creation to impact, so that you have a better evidence base at the time of mandate design. For example, uh, these, uh, elements will be, uh, developed. You can be ready to receive further improvements Over the coming weeks, gather the evidence base on activities that may— that many of you have requested earlier this month so that information is available when intergovernmental organs hold their consultations with a view to helping delegations trace this line from mandate to activity, from activity to resources, and from resources to results. Next week, already during the informal briefing to the General Assembly on the UNHCR initiative, I will provide an update on improved mandate citations in the proposed program budget for 2027. This is the first step towards mandate discipline on our side, being clear about the mandates which ground program and resource requests. At the program and at the sub-program level. It is a step towards better stewardship, ensuring that resources are connected clearly to the mandates that are entrusted to us. However, our efforts will not end there. We will take further steps as part of the implementation of Resolution 80, uh, 251 to help you see both the big pictures and the details. Going forward, when the Secretariat is consulted on a new draft resolution, we will provide the needed information and enhanced support to proponents of draft resolutions and decisions. And please feel free to contact the team at mandates@un.org if you have such requests. And in parallel, we will deepen the analysis of past resolutions and use data analytics with appropriate human review to identify oral statements, PBIs, and activities connected with previous resolutions so that you have granular information as well. The intention again is to make all such information available in one and the same place. Better mandate design begins before adoption with better information at the point of negotiation. Co-chairs, members of the Working Group, in Resolution 80251, you have committed in paragraph 14 to ensure that mandate implementation reviews focus on outcomes and impact rather than only on activities and outputs. And in the same vein, in paragraph 19, You requested the Secretary-General to strengthen and harmonize management for results mechanisms across the UN system, including how results are measured and communicated based on system-wide reporting standards. And in this connection, let me recall the progress to date. A concept for a practical UN system-wide mechanism for management for results has already been developed. A draft action plan has been outlined to improve how the link between mandates, resources, and results can be articulated. Consultations are currently underway to test the concept, practical options, and overall viability of the proposed mechanism. An information brief by the Secretary-General is planned for July, and we look forward to briefing you in the General Assembly. To conclude, all of this is part of the broader mandate lifecycle discipline envisaged by Resolution 82/51. Clear mandate creation, better implementation information, regular review, and stronger system-wide coordination and coherence. Your discussions in the coming weeks will further shape how we provide the related information to the Working Group and to the various intergovernmental organs. It is our role to support those discussions with evidence, data, and implementation analysis, while member states determine the review arrangements that they wish to pursue. This is the disciplines that Resolution 8251 invites us to build. Not a one-time review, but a habit of better collective mandate stewardship. And so before handing it back to the co-chairs, I wanted to share one more update. As you are aware, paragraph 30 of the resolution we are looking at requested the Secretary-General to expand digital tools to support decision-making throughout the mandate life cycle.. And in this context, we would like to invite you to try out the public preview version of transcripts.un.org, which builds on our excellent WebTV infrastructure and other sources to make quick, informal transcripts of public meetings available in one place alongside verbatim records where they are available. You and your teams may find this useful, I have to say, as I have done, as you prepared notes and summaries. It is one more practical example of the same principle: giving delegates better access to the information that they need and when they need it. I thank you for your attention.

Thank you so much for that update, USG Ryder. It's— I have to say, we are quite inspired here as the co-chairs to see how responsive the Secretariat has been and how collaborative they have been in helping us to move forward on implementation of Resolution 8251 in such an expedited way. I think we've come a very long way since the end of March, and we know that the work is ongoing with great enthusiasm on the Secretariat's side, so we are very grateful for that collaboration. You know, we've heard so clearly from Working Group members in our last meeting and in the workshops about the kind of support that Member States needed in order to make informed decisions about mandate creation, implementation, and review, and we are firm in our conviction as co-chairs that this collaboration and dialogue with the Secretariat has to continue. We are committed to facilitating this, and you will hear from us shortly on the arrangements for a dedicated technical briefing in the coming months. Colleagues, returning to the matters at hand, firstly, allow me to thank you all for your engagement and participation in the workshops last week, and again, thanks to the Secretariat colleagues for the extraordinary efforts it took to make those workshops possible. We continue to find these smaller formats to be truly useful to break out of the usual settings and to really exchange views on different sides and different positions. This gives us as co-chairs and everyone else, I think, a better sense of where commonalities lie and where we have work to do to bridge gaps. As we mentioned earlier, we will now use today's meeting as an opportunity for all of us to come back together, having had the benefit of hearing and discussing with colleagues in that smaller format, to share your current thinking on the two tasks in front of us, on criteria and modalities. This will provide us as co-chairs with the guidance we need from you to prepare a more concrete set of proposals on these matters for your consideration. So with that, I open the floor. Please press your microphone buttons if you want to speak, and you'll be given the floor. Given the usual time constraints and in the interests of being able to wrap this up so that we can all engage in the myriad other things that are happening today, we ask you to keep your remarks as concise and succinct as possible to allow as many delegations as possible to take the floor. After we have heard from everyone, Ambassador Bratistad and I will come back to you with some of our reflections and our thinking on next steps. If you will be speaking on behalf of groups, please just indicate to the Secretariat so that we can give you priority.

Okay, we do already have a list. I think I have identified some groups, so I will start by giving the floor to the distinguished representative from Nepal, to be followed by the distinguished representative of Uruguay. Nepal, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, co-chairs, excellencies. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of Least Developed Countries. The group aligns itself with the statement to be delivered by G77 in China shortly. The LDC group thanks the distinguished co-chairs for their dedicated leadership and for the note paper which reflects the substantive exchanges of the preceding workshops. We thank the Under-Secretary-General Guy Ryder for his insightful updates. Co-chairs, the LDC group would like to highlight 5 key issues. First, the group reaffirms that any criteria developed under paragraph 21 of Resolution 80/251 must be clear, objective, and grounded in accurate, impartial data, free from politicization and double standards. The no one-size-fits-all principle must be embedded throughout, and mandates must remain valid until fully implemented or expired. For LDCs, this is not a procedural abstraction. Mandates in development financing, trade preferences, climate resilience, and LDC graduation and smooth transition are of critical importance and must be fully protected. Second, the group underscores that the work of this Working Group must ensure that the development pillar is not disadvantaged while preserving the balance across three pillars of the United Nations as required by paragraph 1 of Resolution 80/251. Any efficiency gains realized through this process must be redeployed to development activities in Programme countries, not absorbed into administrative savings. Third, the review of mandates must remain firmly Member State-led, inclusive and respectful of existing intergovernmental processes and governance arrangements. The Secretary's role is complementary, with clear, analytical, neutral and impartial support. The Group underscores the protection of LDC-specific mandates, including those deriving from Doha Programme of Action, which reflect collective multilateral commitments and must not be subject to unilateral determinations regarding their continued relevance. Fourth, consistent with paragraph 14 of Resolution 80/251, mandate implementation reviews must focus on outcomes and impact, not on mandate elimination as an end in itself. Criteria should target genuine inefficiencies while actively preserving mandates with continuing relevance and unfinished implementation. To speak critically, inadequate resourcing should trigger a resourcing response, not a retirement decision. Fifth, the group shares concerns regarding the coherence of the timeline, developing criteria and modalities before receiving the Secretary-General's analytical reports under Para 16, 18, and 24 risk producing a framework that is not grounded in the full evidence landscape. We call for a properly sequenced process and stress that any proposed pilot exercise must be transparent, time-bound, and without prejudice to the August 2026 deadline. In closing, co-chairs, the LDC group stands ready to engage constructively in this process ahead. We are confident that this process is yet another opportunity to strengthen a mandate architecture that is fit for purpose, adequately resourced, and fully aligned with the needs and priorities of most vulnerable 44 LDCs and the people they represent. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Uruguay, to be followed by the representative of the European Union.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much.

First and foremost, on behalf of Uruguay, I would like to thank you for the information that you shared with us today. And I will move on to reading the G77 and China statement.

I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. At the outset, the group wishes to reiterate its appreciation to the co-chairs, Ambassador Brian Wallace, Permanent Representative of Jamaica, and Ambassador Meret Scheldt, Permanent Representative of Norway, for their work and leadership of the UNAT Work Group II. The Group of 77 and China takes note of the non-paper and appreciates the information provided today regarding the deliberations that took place during the 4 workshops organized by the co-chairs. The Group appreciates that the summary of the views of member states included in the non-paper explicitly recognizes that criteria must be clear, objective, practical, and grounded and evidence-based, impartial data, that we must avoid politicization and double standards, that the diversity of mandates— that is, the no one-size-fits-all principle— must be embedded in any criteria, and that mandates remain valid until fully implemented or expired by their original resolution. The group also appreciates the non-paper recognition of the need to preserve member states' decision-making prerogatives over mandates. The Group of 77 and China wishes to reiterate that the development pillar should maintain its priority under the UNHCR initiative with a focus on how to further enhance support to developing countries. Whenever possible, efficiency gains should be redeployed to development activities in program countries, with a view to fulfilling the UNAT vision of strengthening impact on the ground. In addition, the Group wishes to reiterate its request for a dedicated exchange with the Secretariat, with a view to obtaining accurate, evidence-based, and objective data, as well as impartial expertise and analysis, to support these deliberations and facilitate a better understanding of the mandate's landscape. The Group of 77 and China would welcome further clarity on how the Working Group plans to move forward towards implementation of the mandates contained in paragraphs 21, 22, and 33 of the above-mentioned resolution, and on the timeline for such endeavors. The group would also appreciate a better understanding of how these deliberations on criteria and modalities will interact with the advice and reports requested from the Secretary-General under paragraphs 16, 18, and 24, which are subject to different timelines. In this regard, the Group would welcome information on the expected release date of the report requesting under paragraph 16 concerning the portfolio of mandated reports of the Secretary-General, as well as on the plans of the ad hoc working group in this regard, taking into account that Resolution 80/251 decided that the ad hoc working group should receive and consider this report by the end of July 2026. The Group of 77 and China would also appreciate receiving additional detailed information to better understand the proposal outlined in the non-paper and discussed during the work— the workshops regarding the development of a pilot project aimed at testing review methodologies through a limited set of mandates. The Group would welcome your views on how this type of endeavor would impact the timeline of our work, bearing in mind that Resolution 80/251 mandates the ad hoc working group to develop clear and objective criteria to guide decisions on the renewal, adaptation, merger, replacement, or retirement of GA mandates by the end of August 2026. Excellencies, dear co-chairs, the Group of 77 and China acknowledges your hard work and stands ready to continue to engage constructively with a view to ensuring that mandates remain fit for purpose, that resources are used effectively, and that the priorities of developing countries are fully reflected and advanced. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uruguay and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union, to be followed by the representative of Singapore.

Thank you, Ambassador. Distinguished co-chairs, colleagues, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The European Union remains convinced that our objective should be to develop a practical, action-oriented, and experience-driven toolkit that supports the implementation of the culture shift envisaged in Resolution 80/251 and start implementing it incrementally and as soon as possible. On criteria, a practical checklist will serve as a useful tool to guide review discussions across the United Nations system. Such a checklist must help answer straightforward questions, including whether a mandate con— continues to be actively implemented, whether it still generates measurable outputs or reporting requirements, whether its objectives have already been achieved, whether substantially similar activities are covered elsewhere, whether developments since its adoption have affected its relevance or implementation, and whether budgetary implications associated to this mandate remain relevant in the context of the availability of resources. Mandates whose objectives have been fulfilled or which no longer provide added value should be considered for sunset or for termination. The purpose would be to help ensure that mandates remain impactful, cost-effective, relevant, and fit for purpose by continuously assessing and improving their performance. Thorough reviews would potentially lead to a reduction in the overall number of mandates by reducing overlap and duplication and by, and by retiring outdated or ineffective mandates. That will be welcome since it will reduce the burden on the system and help make the UN more effective. We also reiterate that any criteria should be clear, objective, and evidence-based. Turning to modalities, in order to move towards practical testing and experience-based learning, we support the proposal for a pilot exercise. We should use pilot reviews of mandates from all pillars to test methodologies in a low-risk environment, build confidence among delegations, identify challenges, and generate practical lessons before considering wider application. We could start by identifying low-hanging fruit or theme that could help kickstart this process by identifying areas where early progress can be achieved, helping to build the trust and momentum needed to scale up the process. One idea will be to look at all United Nations observances, including International Days and Weeks, International Years and International Decades, as well as UN anniversaries, as a pilot theme or category. Such a pilot exercise could eventually be a basis for both the modalities for the existing stock review and the review criteria. At the same time, we should not wait for every element to be fully developed before beginning this work. The urgency reflected in Resolution 80/251 calls for an agile and incremental approach. Pilot exercises, Secretariat analysis, and the development of review methodologies can and should evolve in parallel. On thematic or cluster reviews, exploring related mandates within a broader thematic landscape may help identify duplications, gaps, and opportunities for greater coherence while reducing politicization. At the same time, it will be essential to fully respect the principle of balance across the three pillars of the UN. The review process should remain comprehensive and should neither focus disproportionately on nor have a disproportionate impact on any one pillar. In our view, the mandate landscape review offers a great opportunity for such clustered reviews. Moreover, individual member states or groups of member states can always initiate proposals to review certain clusters of mandates. Another issue concerns the role of the Secretariat. A successful review process will require reliable, objective, and data-driven information. Such information should, where possible, include implementation status, reporting requirements, and indicative resource implications, thereby allowing member states to take more informed decisions. We therefore encourage continued efforts to strengthen the mandate registry and develop it into a more comprehensive tool capable of providing a clearer picture of the mandate landscape, performance indicators, and overlaps. Technical briefings and practical demonstrations of these tools could also help build confidence among delegations. And on this regard, we thank you, Chairs, for the brief just provided now by USC Reider, which was very useful, and we look forward to future meetings and reports from the Secretariat. Finally, on institutional arrangements, we see merit in the Working Group serving as a reporting hub that promotes coherence across review efforts. The expertise of the main committees and subsidiary bodies will remain essential. But there is value in ensuring that lessons learned, methodologies, and review outcomes are shared across the system. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore, to be followed by the representative of Australia.

Good morning, co-chairs and friends and colleagues. Let me start by wishing everyone, all of us here, Happy UN Charter Day. On this very significant day, I think it's important that all of us here reflect on the meaning and value of multilateralism, and I think the work that we are doing here in this Working Group on Mandate Implementation Review is not abstract or incidental, but it goes to the heart of making multilateralism meaningful and relevant and ready for the future by delivering results for the people. So I want to thank the co-chairs for their diligence and leadership, and indeed I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the Small States Group, a cross-regional group of small states comprising both developed and developing countries. More than 50 countries have aligned with this statement, and we will make the full list available after the meeting. Co-chairs, for the Small States Group, a strong and effective multilateral system is an existential necessity. Yet the growing volume of mandates, estimated at some 40,000 places, 40,000 places, a disproportionate burden on small delegations with limited resources. Beyond the strain on member states, an ever-expanding mandate base can dilute the UN's focus, stretch resources, and impede effective implementation. Periodic and systematic review is therefore essential to ensure that mandates remain aligned with evolving realities and emerging challenges. Against this backdrop, we view the present discussion on review criteria and modalities as critical to ensuring that the UN remains efficient, effective, and fit for purpose. In this regard, allow me to make three points. First, The SSG supports the development of criteria that are objective, evidence-based, and technically rigorous. We welcome the proposal that any mandate review framework should be grounded in impartial data provided by the Secretariat. For small states, transparency and access to reliable information are essential to navigating the mandate landscape. We therefore agree that criteria for mandate review must be principles-based, and sufficiently flexible to accommodate the diverse nature of mandates, whether normative, thematic, or operational. Such an approach avoids the pitfalls of previous reform efforts and ensures that decisions are guided by impact and outcomes rather than political considerations. Secondly, we are encouraged by the proposal to launch a pilot exercise. This pragmatic, pragmatic, learning-by-doing approach will allow Member States to test and refine review methodologies on a manageable subset of mandates before undertaking a system-wide exercise. The SSG believes that thematic or functional clustering offers the most effective means of identifying overlaps, duplications, gaps, and opportunities for greater coherence. It would also enable Member States to better assess the practical implications of mandate review and develop best practices before scaling up the process. A successful pilot would build the confidence and trust needed to advance this work and demonstrate that mandate review is not an exercise in mandate reduction, but rather a means of ensuring that mandates remain relevant, coherent, and impactful. Thirdly, we agree that the Mandate Registry should be strengthened and leveraged as a central tool for the Working Group's review process. The Registry remains an underutilised asset that can give smaller delegations greater visibility over the mandate landscape and the lifecycle of individual mandates. We support enhancing the Registry with comprehensive performance data and exploring its potential as a reporting platform for subsidiary bodies. Over time, the Registry could also serve as an institutional memory for mandate creation, review, renewal, and sunset decisions. At the same time, Main Committees must embrace the culture of discipline envisaged in Resolution 80/251. Given that a significant proportion of General Assembly mandates are considered within the Main Committees, meaningful and lasting reform must also begin there. Co-Chairs, the SSG remains committed to to engaging constructively in this process. We stand ready to work with all Member States to build a leaner, stronger, and more accountable UN that is equipped to deliver on its mandates and respond to evolving global challenges. The SSG also thanks the co-chairs for their continued leadership of this Working Group, as well as for fostering a transparent, inclusive, and consultative process through our formal meetings and hybrid workshops. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Singapore and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia, to be followed by the representative of Croatia.

Australia, please. Thank you, thank you, co-chair, and to both our co-chairs, thank you for this process. In a personal capacity, let me just say I Absolutely agree with Berhan's acknowledgement of the anniversary of the Charter today, and the work that we're doing here is, I think, fundamental to the future of this institution, so it's such a vital, vital task that we undertake. I've got the honour this morning to speak on behalf of Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and I want to thank you for your leadership and for the NOM paper, which provides a useful and balanced basis for advancing our work. CANZ sees this work as central to delivering on the ambition of Resolution 82/51, a more efficient and effective United Nations grounded in evidence-based decision-making and improved system-wide coherence. The first step in this exercise is to ensure there are review clauses in every new and renewed mandate. We see strong convergence emerging around a practical and workable set of criteria for reviewing of existing mandates. In particular, we support Mexico's proposal that the review focus on three considerations: relevance, impact, and coherence. We also support the checklist suggested by the co-chairs as a flexible and non-prescriptive tool to guide member states. We would encourage inclusion —of additional practical considerations, including whether the resources required to implement the mandate have been adequately assessed and whether they are proportionate to impact; whether mandated outputs, such as reports, are demonstrably used; whether the mandate generates unnecessary or duplicative reporting burdens or meetings; and whether the mandate has been superseded, completed, or overtaken by developments. On modalities, we see 5 essential elements for a credible and effective review process. First, a clear purpose. The review should aim to improve efficiency, coherence, and impact, including by identifying opportunities to streamline reporting, consolidate mandates, reduce unnecessary administrative burdens, and improve overall mandate delivery while safeguarding core normative functions. Second, a strong foundation in evidence. We reiterate the critical importance of strengthening and expanding the Secretariat's mandate registry and ensuring it includes key information such as mandate age, origin, legal status, implementing entity, resource implications, reporting requirements, outputs, and overlap with other mandates. This information is essential to enable informed, objective decision-making. Third, a cluster-based approach. We strongly support reviewing mandates in thematic clusters rather than individually. This will allow Member States to better identify duplication and fragmentation and consider opportunities for consolidation thereby improving coherence and impact. Fourth, a pragmatic pilot phase. We see merit in beginning with a limited pilot focused on a manageable set of mandates to ensure early progress and refine our methodology. This could include General Assembly plenary mandates, uh, and, uh, others as appropriate. Fifth, a sense of urgency. We need to set a time frame for the review. We suggest starting in the 81st session of the General Assembly. While Secretariat inputs will be critical, many delegations have underscored that work cannot wait. We therefore encourage parallel progress, advancing criteria and modalities while continuing to engage closely with forthcoming Secretariat analysis, including the Secretary-General's review of inactive, duplicative, or fully implemented mandates. In this context, we encourage the Secretary-General to provide timely advice on mandate clustering, implementation status, and possible collective review mechanisms to support member states in undertaking informed and efficient reviews. Co-chairs, in conclusion, CANZ looks forward to engaging constructively with you and all member states to carry this extremely important work forward. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia and now give the floor to the distinguished the representative of Croatia, to be followed by the representative of Algeria.

Croatia. Thank you for organizing this meeting on criteria and stock review modalities. We also appreciate the workshops which helped us examine key issues in depth and hear the views of other delegations. Croatia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, and I would like to add 3 points in my national capacity. First, the implementation of Resolution 8251 is a system-wide exercise. It must cover mandates across all three pillar— UN pillars in a balanced way, supported by solid data and analytical tools. Second, close cooperation with the Secretariat remains essential to fully understand the current mandate landscape. The mandate registry should be strengthened and developed into a comprehensive, data-driven resource. A refined checklist would also help guide the review. And third, while the Working Group plays an important role, the main committees should remain central. They engage with mandates regularly and are best placed to assess implementation and advise on how mandates should evolve within their areas of competence. We look forward to continuing our work with the EU co-chairs and to ensure this process is as concrete and useful as possible.

I thank you very much. I thank the distinguished representative of Croatia and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Algeria, to be followed by the representative of the Russian Federation.

Thank you, Madam Chair, for the statement delivered by Uruguay. On behalf of G77 and China and wishes to add few elements. At the outset, Algeria believes that any review of mandates must be guided by clear safeguards. It must preserve the exclusive prerogative of member states in deciding the future of mandates. Particular attention should also be given to mandates grounded in the Charter of the United Nations, as well as those addressing situations with implications for international peace and security. With regard to criteria, Algeria suggests four main elements. First, on continued relevance, the review should assess whether the mandates still respond to a valid need or priority and whether its termination or weakening would create a political, development, legal, or accountability gap. Second, on implementation status, the review should determine whether the mandate has been fully or partially implemented or remains pending, and whether delays are due to external factors such as political stale— stalemate or financial constraint. Third, effectiveness and impact. The review should assess the concrete contribution of the mandate, including its preventive value in avoiding conflict escalation, violation, and other adverse developments. Fourth, duplication and complementarity. The review should identify genuine duplication while recognizing that some overlap may be justified when it reflects the cross-cutting nature of an issue and adds value through different perspective. In conclusion, Algeria believes that this process should be gradual, evidence-based, and member-state-driven. Its objective should be to improve coherence and effectiveness while preserving mandate delivery and the intergovernmental character of the United Nations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Algeria and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation, to be followed by the representative of Japan. Russia.

Plogodaryu asso. Thank you, co-chairs.

Thank you for giving us the floor. For the paper we have submitted for the consideration of member states, we consider this as a useful basis for further consideration, for further discussion. At the same time, we are of the view that what is necessary is that we lay down certain points of principle. First of all, developing the criteria, the methodology, and subsequent use of any approaches to mandate review needs to be fully under the member states' control. The role of the Secretariat is in providing objective, neutral, and factual information technical support, data, but this support should not prejudge or predetermine the political or the substantive assessment of the mandate. Let me repeat, any decisions on the mandates are the exclusive prerogative of member states. Second key issue is the scope. Of the review and the criteria. We remain of the view that we need to work out a general understanding of how, um, paragraph 25 of Resolution 8251 is going to be understood. Now, in order to exclude risk that the review will also apply to mandates which we factually agreed to exclude from the process. As many delegations present here, we also think that it is important that we move stage by stage, gradually. Before the criteria should be applied to a wider range of mandates, we consider the idea of having a pilot implementation of the criteria to a number of mandates, which— and in our view, we think that human rights mandates, for example, could come in here, amongst which duplication is something that's fairly widespread. Decisions on specific mandates should ultimately be made by the relevant intergovernmental bodies which establish those mandates. In line with their competency and their own rules of procedure. And I also cannot but comment the issues having to do with the establishing of a checklist. Ideally, this kind of a tool disciplines the discussion and compels us to look at facts. Rather than political preferences. The important thing here is to make sure that the checklist does not create the false impression of objectivity. The answer yes or no given to a formal question does not always disclose the political, legal, or the normative importance of a mandate. It's important to make sure that we do not approach the issue of duplication mechanically. Not all coincidence of themes or functions is an unnecessary duplication, and we have already mentioned that earlier. And finally, we think this process should not be an exercise to reduce the number of mandates as a goal in itself. The goal is to increase clarity, coherence, and most importantly, the quality of mandate implementation. I would like to express thanks to USG Ryder especially for the attention he constantly pays to the work of the group. And once again, immediately I would like to react to what was As I said, in particular, on the issue of the merger of mandates on construction, the important thing here is to make sure that the mandate on— the current mandate on the major one on SAP should remain a separate mandate. We think that this is an important point. We agree The mandate registry resource need to be broadened to make sure that it becomes an effective mechanism. Thank you very much for your attention.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. And just to clear what USG Ryder actually said, I think he talked about a possible merger of the reporting on the construction mandates into one rather than many reports on a very similar— but not to do anything on the mandates itself, but on the reporting of it. That was my understanding, but we will have that clarified. So moving on, let me give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan, to be followed by the representative of Finland.

Thank you, Madam and Mr. Co-Chairs. At the outset, I would like to thank USG Guy Lai for his updates on the Secretariat's efforts, which was very useful. We also reiterate our sincere appreciation for the Co-Chairs' efforts on the NOMPAPR, which serves as a valuable foundation for our discussions on criteria and modalities. As for criteria, while we had anticipated a zero draft for the criteria, we are keen to understand the future discussion direction and if such a draft is envisioned. Later. From Japan's perspective, paragraph 24 of Resolution 80/51, specifically inactive, duplicative, or fully implemented, offers a robust framework for establishing criteria. The mandate reviews aims to identify duplication using criteria as technical tools. The Secretariat's technical support is crucial for member states to grasp the overall mandate landscape. We respectfully suggest that the Secretariat could share criteria that it would use in reviews under paragraphs 18 and 24. Detailed information on posts and budgetary allocation for each mandate, enabling information— informed decisions by us. We generally agree with the checklist approach proposed in the NOM paper, especially items 1 to 4, as they align its paragraph 24, which I just mentioned. We wish to offer some observation regarding the options— options part in the NOM paper. Firstly, regarding a full formal working group, we question if a permanent WG— working group— is the most efficient mechanism if its main role is solely reporting hub. We suggest introducing a corresponding indicator into the mandate registry as a possible alternative. Given past opposition in the informal ad hoc working group, a clear explanation for essential tasks for a full formal WG is needed for thorough discussion. Secondly, we request clarification of the meaning of find solutions before bringing them to broader assembly in the third point. Thirdly, concerning the scope in the fourth point, if it refers to paragraph 25 of Resolution 80/258, 5.1. The SG's advice is essential. However, concerning modalities, we think that waiting for the SG's advice could affect the resolution's timeline, to which we are obliged to stick. Japan continues to support the co-chair and looks forward to achieving concrete results. In this working group. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Finland to be followed by the representative of the Maldives. Finland.

I would like to begin by congratulating both co-chairs on assuming the important responsibility— of guiding our collective effort to streamline the mandate work of the United Nations. Finland aligns with the statement delivered by the EU, and I will make some remarks in national capacity. Finland welcomes the ongoing efforts to rationalize the mandate landscape, both with regard to new mandates and the review of existing ones. We consider the concept note and the templates for drafting new mandates to be very useful and practical tools. Now it is essential that the systematic use of those tools becomes normalized. Going forward, member states should, as a standing practice, engage with those instruments in a substantive and meaningful manner when tabling new proposals. The completion of the concept note should not become a mechanical exercise. Strengthening our mandate framework must be undertaken in a rational and efficient way. In doing so, we should remain mindful of the need to avoid creating additional burdens for the Secretariat, particularly in the context of constrained resources. As we move forward with implementing our shared commitments, it would be beneficial to to periodically take stock of experiences with the concept notes and templates. Such reflections could help us jointly assess their impact on both the quality and quantity of new mandates and identify areas where further refinement may be beneficial. Turning to existing mandates, the review constitutes an important next step. This should be approached as a be a holistic and comprehensive exercise, ideally conducted along thematic lines. In our view, the review should take a system-wide perspective, avoiding a case-by-case review of individual mandates. We support the proposal to initiate a pilot project in this regard. This could help establish effective working methods and provide evidence of impact before for broader implementation. Such an approach would allow us to refine methodology— methodologies and ensure the overall success of the exercise. Finally, in the spirit of efficiency and effectiveness, the objectives of the UNAID reform effort, Finland supports strengthening this working group by continuing discussions on mandate review within this forum. We believe it would be counterproductive if reform efforts were to lead to an increase rather than a reduction in the number of bodies and meetings. For this reason, we do not support the establishment of a standalone working group. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Finland and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Maldives to be followed by the representative of Argentina.

Maldives. The Maldives thank you for the Nunn Paper and for your efforts to structure our discussion on criteria and modalities. On criteria, we support a practical and evidence-based approach. Mandates should be addressed against continued relevance, implementation status, outcome,: impact, duplication and added value, reporting utilities, resourcing, and feasibility. But these criteria must be applied carefully. First, mandates should remain valid unless and until member states decide otherwise. We should not support automatic sunsetting, automatic deletion, or automatic retirement. The age of a mandate should not by itself itself be treated as evidence that it is obsolete. Some older mandates remain foundational. Second, weak implementation should not be treated as proof that a mandate is unnecessary. In cases weak implementation reflects inadequate resources, unclear responsibilities, fragmented coordination, or unrealistic timelines, where a mandate remains relevant, the answer should be to improve implementation. Implementation, not retire the mandate. Third, duplication must be defined precisely. Thematic overlap is not the same as duplication. Mandates may address related issues while serving different political, normative, analytical, operational purposes. A mandate should be considered duplicative only where it is objective, implementing entirely outputs, reporting audience, and periodically and substantially the same as other mandates. Fourth, we must preserve balance across the three pillars. Development mandates should not be weakened in the name of efficiency. For smaller states, CEDS mandates provide visibility, analysis, accountability, and a pathway to translate intergovernmental commitments into practical supports. In all these modalities, we support a transparent, inclusive, and manageable process. The first step should be a clear scoping exercise including the screening out of the categories excluded under paragraph 25. The Secretariat can provide factual and impartial mapping, but the mapping must be non-perspective and validated by member states before conclusions are drawn. We also support thematic— but clustering should be a tool for discussion, not a presumption in favor of merger, replacement, or retirement. Similarly, changes reporting to periodically should be case-by-case, not automatic. Finally, this process must not place inappropriate burdens on smaller delegations, reopen agreed normative languages, or force packages, deals, that trade acceptable improvements or for problematic retirements. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Maldives and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Argentina, to be followed by the representative of Mexico.

Argentina. Muchas gracias. Thank you very much, co-chairs. A very good morning to you. Thank you very much for convening this meeting and for circulating the non-paper and for the discussion in the workshops, uh, at the library. We would like to take advantage of this opportunity to reiterate some of the elements that we've already mentioned in previous meetings. Additionally, comments made by the G77. As we said before, we believe that the key word for the work before us in developing the criteria and modalities is objectivity. Any framework or mechanism that we use to support a decision-making process should be based on technical perspectives that allow us to identify the most objective— in the most objective way the necessary elements to assess— to do the assessment that we member states must do. And as we've said, the reports of the Secretariat will be very important in that endeavor. They should be technical, objective, impartial, and they should fully reflect the provisions of Paragraph 25 of the resolution. We thus appreciate the briefing that was made by Guy Ryder on this. We have proposed an objective element that might be used in the analysis. This is the budgetary impact that is created by every mandate from all of the sources of financing, not necessarily just from one, from from all of them, and based on this, what are the duplications or the overlapping— overlaps that could arise from that? It is also worth reiterating one of the principles that we need to keep in mind. One of them is— and in fact, it's been mentioned by many delegations— is that mandates must remain valid and relevant until they're implemented. This is in paragraph 20 of the resolution. And with this, we also have to be cautious vis-à-vis the proposals to review mandates based only on how old the mandate is or subjective perceptions by delegations on what could be considered inactive or obsolete. Another issue that is essential in our view is the proper and full implementation of the provisions of paragraph 25, particularly relating to modalities, the review modalities that are contemplated in Article 33 of, uh, Roman IV. As the reason for this is because we want to maintain a technical focus and avoid any kind of politicization of debates. Finally, we think we have to avoid classifications between what could be considered duplicative on the one hand, or on the other hand, cross-cutting, as there are always different views of this. Somebody might consider something duplicative, another might think it's cross-cutting. This is why we highlight the need for a technical and objective focus on these topics. Also, as mentioned before, there is no single approach. There are a variety of mandates, and we must consider the various different specificities that each Assembly Committee has, as well as the Special Committees have, In terms of next steps, we understand that we could move forward in the drafting of an initial draft. That's a valuable exercise. We also need to strengthen the tools, the evaluation tools, the registration of— or the list of mandates has been mentioned by Mr. Ryder, where we will be able to obtain the technical and objective mechanisms in order to identify overlaps and duplications. And based on this, we can begin working on an exercise to group mandates when necessary, and we can assess that and consider a gradual step— step-by-step approach, as has been mentioned by some delegations, starting with the least controversial matters. This would lead to to pilot experiences that will allow us to fine-tune the methodology, and this would also foster trust and understanding among the various delegations and in the process itself. Please allow me to also share a thought with you that's off script. We've talked a little bit earlier on today about the importance of discipline. In the creation and implementation of mandates, and we have supported that. And we think it is important for all member states to be disciplined when we develop mandates. And in meetings and in the various processes, as we've said on several occasions, this discipline also must be followed by the Secretariat, not just by member states. It is a discipline that must characterize the entire system, and we have many examples of initiatives and summits and processes that have been launched by the Secretariat. And we, in fact, have meetings in July, high-level meetings that will be held that have been promoted by the Secretariat without any intergovernmental mandate. Discipline is an exercise that is shared between the membership and the Secretariat. So if only one part is disciplined and the other isn't, that would also undermine trust or the cultural change that we are all trying to promote in these efforts. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico, to be followed by the representative of China. So, Mexico.

Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much, co-chairs. Mexico recognizes the great efforts made by both co-facilitators of the Working Group, Jamaica and Norway, on the implementation of the General Assembly's mandates, and we greatly value the working document that was presented to us and that we are reviewing now. As well as the diligent organization of hybrid workshops that allowed us to exchange proposals in order to define criteria and modalities for the implementation of the mandates. Based on the multiple exchanges that were held during the hybrid workshops, Mexico would like to highlight the following points related only to the criteria and the review modalities. First, for Mexico, the criteria should be differentiated based on the goals that are established. Second, the three main criteria for evaluating the effect of individual mandates— modalities should be relevance, impact, and cohesion, as was mentioned by the distinguished representative of Australia. Third, the support criteria or the secondary criteria should be non-duplication, the status of implementation, as well as the operative obsolescence of mandates, as has already been mentioned by previous speakers who already took the floor. The three review criteria of the mandate system in general Collectively should be efficiency, effectiveness, and sustainability. Mexico— this is my third point— thinks it's valuable to implement a pilot phase as a mechanism in order to evaluate methodologies and identify possible areas where we could make an adjustment before broadening the process. 4. When it comes to modalities on mandates and the review of them, Mexico would agree that the review exercise should be carried out by the bodies that created them, and each body should present results on— to the ad hoc working group. 5. Mexico would— considers that the countries or groups of countries that proposed mandates should on a voluntary basis consider the frequency with which they present their resolutions or reports, as well as the degree of fulfillment of the mandates and the added value of its annual presentation. Finally, Mexico, like other delegations, recognizes the need to enjoy the technical support from the Secretariat. This is why we value the progress that has been made on digital platforms reforms, even though we do need to constantly review and update the information presented. Thank you very much, co-chairs.
I thank the distinguished representative of Mexico and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China, to be followed by the representative of the United Kingdom.

China. Co-chairs, thank you for convening today's meeting. For striving to advance the work of the AHWG on mandate implementation review. Equally, I thank USG Ryder for his briefing and the Secretariat for its diligent work. China aligns itself with a statement by Uruguay on behalf of G77 and China. We also thank the co-chairs for preparing the NAM paper on the criteria and modalities for the mandate implementation review, which quite comprehensively reflects the views of member states and sets out important principles including ensuring member state leadership and national ownership, preserving the balance across the three pillars, respecting diversity of mandates, avoiding one-size-fits-all, and opposing politicization and double standards, thus offering in offering a useful basis for the next phase of discussion. I wish to further emphasize the following points. First, lessons learned from previous review exercises must be fully taken into account. The review should ultimately enhance effective mandate delivery by systematically identifying mandates that genuinely require streamlining and objectively analyzing factors affecting their implementation instead of becoming an exercise of reduction for reduction's sake and getting into politicized debates over mandates themselves. Second, development remains the foremost concern of the vast majority of member states, particularly developing countries. The review should fully reflect the needs and priorities of member states, pay particular attention to any implications for the development pillar and development mandates and ensure strengthened institutional and resource support for implementing the 2030 Agenda. Third, while maintaining member state leadership, the support of the Secretariat is essential. The Secretariat should provide objective, impartial, and evidence-based analysis and recommendations, thereby offering a sound basis for decision-making by member states. Fourth, on criteria, China is of the view that it might be more practical to focus on areas of convergence and develop a set of broad guiding principles and criteria framework that could serve as a reference for the main committees of the GA and their subsidiary bodies to be adapted and applied in line with their circumstances and expertise. Fifth, on modalities, the main committees and their subsidiary bodies may draw upon the Secretary-General's recommendations in conducting reviews in accordance with their respective mandates and decision-making processes while avoiding duplication with the current intergovernmental review process. For other mandates, China supports making full use of existing mechanisms mechanisms and processes. China stands ready to continue working with the co-chairs and all parties to support the group in successfully completing its mandate within the agreed framework timeframe, ensuring that the mandate implementation review proceeds steadily in the right direction. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of China and now give the floor to the distinguished Representative of the United Kingdom, to be followed by the Representative of Brazil.

Thank you, co-chairs, for the very helpful workshops last week and to having USG Ryder join us today. I think his responses to our requests for further information across mandate implementation and reporting templates, uh, the registry and the results mechanism is very encouraging. So really welcome that, um, and we look forward to the dedicated briefings and the further advice to come. Um, just to underline a few points, um, so I think others have said, and we agree, that the SecGen's advice will be critical for determining the scope of modalities for the review of remaining mandates and will help chart the clearest path for member state agreement. Um, so we welcome receiving that as soon as is possible. Um, we agree with others that the best place to start is a pilot with a limited set of mandates based on the Secretary-General's recommendations, and then we can expand if that's successful. We also welcome this group receiving examples from other bodies on how they have approached reviewing mandates so we can learn lessons. On criteria, um, we agree that the mandate review should look across all three pillars of the UN's work holistically ethically and objectively. It should tackle duplication, promote efficiency and coherence, and of course focus on implementation and impact. Um, on modalities, we agree with others on the suggested thematic clustering of mandates so we don't look at them in isolation. Um, the mandate registry is going to be really critical for that as well, so we can take a full stock of implementation and what is unique or what overlaps. And I know there's various views on this, but we are open to other means of bringing mandates into scope for review, such as those that don't receive budgetary support or have been inactive for, uh, 20 or more years. And just finally, we'd really encourage strong collaboration between this working group and the presidents of ECOSOC, the General Assembly, the chairs of committees, to ensure that we can embed and implement the recommendations that are coming out and the templates across the UN's work. I think that's really important. We have an opportunity this year to use those, to implement them, and so it's really important that we all actively do that so this work becomes real. So we're very committed to continue to work with you all, this group, you as co-chairs, to take that forward. Thank you. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil, to be followed by the representative of South Africa, who will be the last speaker unless someone else presses the button.

So, Brazil. Thank you very much. Good morning to co-chairs and to colleagues. As usual, I associate myself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of G77. And, um, my delegation does agree with many of the points that have made— been made by colleagues, in particular by the Russian delegation, on some of the cautions needed. Um, just a few points. One, obviously, we, we do thank you for the non-paper. We do thank USG Ryder for the briefing. And on the briefing I'd like to thank the Secretariat for, if I understood correctly, his briefing and the, um, and what we heard in the last hybrid workshop, that the Secretariat is making progress in providing or collecting the kinds of information we need to undertake this exercise as As we all know, currently the mandate registry is not prepared to provide member states with all the information we need, especially when trying to compare mandates, and much less when it comes to implementation, actually what was actually achieved or not in the implementation of the mandates. Two quick words on modality. As many others have said, and I think there is a growing consensus that the review should be in the hands of the bodies that have mandated, so no centralized, let's say, instance of review. This obviously has an impact on the way business is conducted in the subsidiary bodies or the General Assembly, etc. And I do support what the UK mission said in terms of full coordination with the other bodies to make sure that whatever implications there are from the resolution are fully taken into consideration. As to criteria, I just wanted to briefly comment one thing that you mentioned in your non-paper and has been mentioned by delegations, which is the, the criterion of relevance. I mean, this, this seems obvious. Nobody wants to be doing irrelevant things, but as always, the devil is in the detail.— and especially when it comes to reviewing the stock of mandates. I think that if we delve into this particular criterion, we will get bogged down. We will not be able to complete our work because there will be probably 193 views on the relevance of any given mandate, and we will be unwillingly and likely repeating the failure of 20 years ago. Obviously, there is an aspect of relevance that I think is objective, which is if the mandate, for example, has been completed, it's been— it has outlasted its mandate, its utility, then obviously it should be retired on the basis of, as many delegations have said, objective criteria, and I'll go back to the issue of information. And my final word is, as many other delegations also agree, that we should try to pilot some of these things so that we give ourselves a reality check. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa, to be followed by the representative of Iran. South Africa.

Thank you, co-chairs, and once again, thank you for all your efforts and work undertaken as well as the non-paper that you've provided us, which I think is really moving us forward and helpful. My delegation aligns with the statement made by the G77, and then also in terms of what we've heard today, we were happy to hear a lot of positive approaches, obviously some guarded, and we are all cautious in terms of protecting— that's what is important to us. But from our perspective as well, we were just I would just like to add a few words of caution. We understand that there's a need to move quickly and to look at this whole load of mandates that sits out there, but we would appeal for an incremental approach and looking at this carefully. We should be careful also not that perfection becomes the enemy of the good. We've got a good process going on here. We've got good— and delegations are open to making this work, but we need to find a practical way to make this work. And starting off, and you've spoken about a pilot project, so we agree with many of the points made that the review should be done within the bodies that matter. With them. And we need to find a practical instrument whereby to do this. And my delegation has consistently asked that we keep on focusing on mandate implementation review. I know we then drop the implementation and start speaking about reviews and getting rid of stuff, but we need to be cautious. There's a lot of interest around the room and very— and a lot of delegations are very cautious about where we're going and how we're approaching this. So we need to preserve this goodwill by taking, for instance, the 81st session coming up and looking at the committee work and asking the Secretariat that each and every of the resolution reports that will be issued for the resolutions that we will be considering, that on each and every one of those, there is a section on where the implementation is of those specific resolutions, and that we start in a minimalist approach with, say, the six committees, and we take that as our pilot, because what we're doing here is something totally new, and none of our colleagues in the six committees are going to approach it in the same way. They're all going to have different understandings what this committee is thinking and what we're saying, even if we coordinate very well in our missions. So we need to find a way to make this very practical, to start to have a starting point, and then also this committee or mechanism or what we're going to decide to do with this will be very relevant in terms of not just being a hub, but also looking that across the different areas of work, and we've heard about the pillars, so all the pillars should be represented in this committees and that we make sure that we have a standard approach across committees in terms of how we're looking at mandate implementation review, because our understandings even in the room differ from what we understand from that term. All of us think differently. So once we start getting going on this, then I think it will crystallize more and we will, you know, speak to each other and see that we have different beliefs and then we find each other. But I think we need to start incrementally in a limited manner and then need to start to get the message out and then revert back to this structure in order to see are we on the right way or not. In terms of the clustering, I'm not sure how that's going to work. If my delegation is presented with a cluster of resolutions, where do I start? And then if the Secretariat suggests something, I need to— we need to interrogate whether we agree with what the that the Secretariat agrees with, and many delegations will have different views on that. So the clustering I get, but I don't think that is a practical way to start working on that. We can get to clustering eventually. I'm not saying that that's not something that cannot be done, but we first need to put some mechanism in place that we are all on the same page and understand what we are doing, and maybe a way to do that is to start very practically through the 81st session in the committee work and let the Secretariat tell us what the implementation of each of the resolutions that we are busy working on, what is that like, and then we take it from there. So our appeal would just be to be incremental and then hopefully all of that will make sure that we are even-handed, it's not politicized, we are dealing with what's on the table, and then gradually we will find our way over because for us this process is really important. We think we— the decision we made was really groundbreaking and in the UN you don't make You don't take giant leaps. It's all incremental. And as soon as you try to take a giant leap, it falls apart. So let's preserve what we have and also to keep the goodwill that we see in the room, and there are great ideas in the room, but sometimes we just might maybe have to temper them or see how we structure them going forward. It doesn't mean these are bad ideas. It's maybe sometimes just how we take them forward into in terms of what sequencing we do. So that would be our appeal. But thank you very much for the good work you're doing and for the energy you're putting into this. We really appreciate it.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran, to be followed by the representative of Brazil.

Thank you, Madam Chair. In the name of God, the most compassionate, the most merciful. Thank you, co-chairs, for preparing the known paper and convening this meeting. Also, thanks and appreciation for the US Ryder for his comprehensive briefing on the last updates on UNADTT. The Islamic Republic of Iran aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of Group of 77 and China. Regarding the substance, we agree that any review of the existing stock of General Assembly mandates should be guided by the principle principle of relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, and coherence. At the same time, it is essential that the review fully respects the sovereign prerogatives of member states and the intergovernmental nature of mandate decision-making. In our view, the central question should not be how many mandates can be reduced or consolidated, but rather whether mandates continue to serve the purposes and principles principles of the Charter of the United Nations and respond to the priorities and needs identified by member states with more quality and clarity. The mere fact that a mandate is longstanding or has seen limited implementation in recent years should not automatically make it a candidate for consolidation or merger. Its continued relevance and the reasons for its level of implementation should be carefully assessed before any such determination is made. Particular attention should be given to the extent to which mandates contribute to strengthening international cooperation, supporting development, promoting capacity building, and addressing the needs of developing countries, including those facing special external pressures or challenges. The review should also assess whether mandate facilitate equitable access to technical assistance, knowledge sharing, and international cooperation in line with the commitment to leave no country behind. We further believe that the review process should seek to avoid duplication and fragmentation, strengthen complementarities across the United Nations system, and promote the efficient use of resources. However, such efforts must not come at the expense of development priorities or mandates that remain relevant to the needs of developing countries. We attach particular importance to maintaining a clear distinction between the decision-making role of member states and the supporting role of the Secretariat. The Secretariat has an important contribution to make through the provision of objective, impartial, evidence-based and technical analysis. However, its role should remain strictly supportive nature and should not prejudice or predetermine decisions that belong exclusively to member states. Transparency, neutrality, objectivity, and respect for intergovernmental oversight must remain guiding principles throughout this process. Finally, the pilot with a limited number of missions option is practically appealing because it entails relatively low risk and can can help build capacity comparing to other options. However, it raises a key concern, the possibility that pilot could evolve into a permanent standard without the cautious approach that we needed. The things that has been discussed and mentioned by some member states, and we think that to consider this fact is an important issue and priority for all of us. As working group to make this procedure go and advance. Thank you so much.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran and now give the floor back to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Thank you, co-chair. I won't apologize for asking the floor again, just in our contribution to make it as interactive as possible, and thank you very much for the generosity of giving me the floor. Just to follow up on the intervention by the delegation of South Africa on clustering, I fully agree with him when he says that there are, at least to me, seems, there seems to be, to exist plenty of views of what clustering is. And in the process, should you develop your own understanding based on your own thinking and consultations, I think it would be quite useful for delegations to, um, to learn from you. Um, just a quick word on, on this. Um, on one hand, I think it's inevitable to have some clustering from a substantive point of view, meaning, uh, if we'll be reviewing resolutions on technical assistance, it makes sense to have them clustered in one big group so that we can compare —regarding, for example, the issue of duplicity, or et cetera. So again, at least in my view, I don't see how we can get out of this cluster in this sense of simply organizing resolutions thematically so that we can compare them.
